column22: Being centered, it obstructed an important region of my field of view, including making it difficult to read the directional guidance arrow. It was nice to be able to direct my physical view as needed to adjust my positioning, though.
column28: The framerate suffered every few moments as the image detection was running. Since the windows could not update often, they shifted away from whatever they detected as soon as my head turned, so it was difficult to tell what was being detected. Also, many false positives on random objects in my environment.
column34: For my play area, the detection threshold was a little too high, so it constantly showed a region of the floor and nearby objects around me in my lower peripheral; however, that wasn't too disruptive, since it was too low in my vision to seriously interfere with my task. Preventing objects outside of the play area from being detected may help.
column48: Room 3's Detection Window, due to technical limitations, appeared the most unexpectedly and with the least obvious reasons, due to the window shifting away from the triggers when my head turned even a little bit. Larger windows or some kind of lightweight object tracking could potentially smooth this out. Preventing objects outside of the play area from being displayed may also help.
column53: Somehow account for approach velocity, distance, object type, and play area, and show a smooth cutout of relevant objects with smooth transitions to limit disruption to immersion.
